question: What is the main goal of using the nursing process in everyday clinical practice?

options.A: To replace the need for direct communication with physicians
options.B: To fulfill mandatory hospital paperwork requirements only
options.C: To determine the financial cost of hospital stays
options.D: To provide a clear, step-by-step guide for giving personal patient care

explanation: Think of the nursing process as your trusty roadmap! It helps you organize your thoughts and actions so you can safely meet each patient's unique health needs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why do we call the nursing process a dynamic cycle instead of a straight line?

options.A: Patient care plans never change once they are initially written
options.B: Nurses must continuously check and update care as the patient's condition changes
options.C: Hospital administrators require the steps to be repeated every hour
options.D: The steps can be performed in any random order depending on the nurse's mood

explanation: Patient health goes up and down! Because of this, you'll constantly flow back and forth between checking on them, planning, and seeing if your care worked. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which of these is a clear example of objective data?

options.A: A feeling of dizziness upon standing up quickly
options.B: A body temperature reading of 38.5 degrees Celsius
options.C: A statement of anxiety about upcoming surgery
options.D: A patient reporting a dull ache in the lower back

explanation: Objective data is what you can actually see, touch, or measure yourself (like a thermometer reading), unlike feelings that only the patient can tell you about. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h2)

question: Why is double-checking (validating) your data such an important step in assessment?

options.A: It is required by law to be completed within fifteen minutes of admission
options.B: It allows the nurse to delegate all future care tasks to unlicensed staff
options.C: It ensures your information is correct before you make clinical choices
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any subjective patient interviews

explanation: Validating helps you catch mix-ups or misunderstandings early, so you don't build a care plan on the wrong information. Always good to double-check! [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h2)

question: How is a nursing diagnosis different from a medical diagnosis?

options.A: A medical diagnosis describes how a patient feels emotionally
options.B: A nursing diagnosis focuses on how the patient responds to health conditions
options.C: A medical diagnosis can only be made by a registered nurse
options.D: A nursing diagnosis identifies the exact pathology of a disease

explanation: You've got this! A medical diagnosis names the disease itself (like malaria), while a nursing diagnosis focuses on how the patient reacts to it (like feeling exhausted or in pain). [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h3)

question: A patient with a broken leg complains of throbbing pain and winces when moving. Which option is a great nursing diagnosis focus?

options.A: Fracture of the right tibia and fibula bones
options.C: Surgical repair of the lower leg bones
options.D: Acute pain related to physical tissue trauma

explanation: Spot on! 'Acute pain' describes the patient's human response to their injury, which is exactly what we as nurses diagnose and manage. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h3)

question: When you have several nursing diagnoses at once, which one should you tackle first?

options.A: Risk for impaired skin integrity on the left heel
options.B: Knowledge deficit regarding a new low-salt diet
options.C: Mild anxiety regarding the upcoming hospital discharge
options.D: Ineffective breathing pattern with oxygen saturation at 85%

explanation: Airway and breathing always come first! Life-threatening issues take top priority over comfort, teaching, or emotional needs every single time. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h4)

question: What makes an expected outcome (goal) well-written?

options.A: It must be measurable and time-bound
options.B: It should describe what the nurse will do
options.C: It should be as broad as possible
options.D: It must focus on hospital routines

explanation: Goals need clear targets and deadlines (like 'patient will walk to the door by tomorrow') so you can easily tell if they were actually reached. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic example of an independent nursing intervention?

options.A: Ordering a diagnostic blood panel for a newly admitted patient
options.B: Setting up a surgical tray for a bedside chest tube insertion
options.C: Repositioning a bedbound patient every two hours to prevent pressure sores
options.D: Administering a prescribed dose of intravenous antibiotic medication

explanation: As a nurse, you don't need a doctor's order to turn a patient to protect their skin! That is something you can assess and do independently. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why should you quickly check on your patient right before you carry out a planned intervention?

options.A: To confirm that the planned action is still safe and necessary for them right now
options.B: To rewrite the entire medical diagnosis from the beginning
options.C: To make sure the physician is standing nearby to supervise the nursing care
options.D: To ensure that all hospital equipment has been paid for in advance

explanation: Patients change fast! What was a great plan an hour ago might need tweaking if their condition shifts. Always assess before you act. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the main thing you do during the evaluation phase of the nursing process?

options.A: Gathering initial demographic data during the patient's admission
options.B: Writing out shift handoff notes without checking patient progress
options.C: Comparing the patient's actual health status against the expected outcomes
options.D: Formulating brand new medical diagnoses for the physician to sign

explanation: Evaluation is like checking your scorecard. You look back at the goals you set and ask, 'Did our care help the patient reach them?' [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h6)

question: What should you do if your patient's expected outcome is NOT met during evaluation?

options.A: Examine the data and revise the care plan to better address the patient's needs
options.B: Wait for the patient to figure out a new solution on their own
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately since the hospital stay is finished
options.D: Pretend the goal was met and document normal findings in the chart

explanation: Unmet goals aren't a failure—they're just a sign to put on your detective hat, figure out what's not working, and adjust your plan! [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h6)

question: In the popular SBAR communication tool used by healthcare workers, what does the letter 'B' stand for?
explanation: SBAR is a handy way to report patient info! 'B' stands for Background, giving the listener the essential history leading up to the current moment. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h7)

question: Why is proper nursing documentation so legally critical for patient care?

options.A: It allows patients to diagnose their own illnesses at home
options.B: It serves as a legal record proving what care was delivered to the patient
options.C: It replaces the need for nurses to talk to doctors in person
options.D: It guarantees that the hospital will receive extra government funding

explanation: Remember the golden rule in nursing: if you didn't chart it, you didn't do it! Your notes are legal proof of the safe care you provided. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h7)
